Fair enough- though I do think that game journalism is just as relevant in the age of social media. Is it getting watered down thanks to everybody having a blog? Maybe a bit. Maybe a lot. But is it losing relevance? I don't think so. Of course I'll be biased in favor of game journalism, I'd like very much for my job to stay relevant, but only insofar as I am useful and insightful. I'm an independent journalist and believe me, there's a lot of temptation to give in and make clickbait for hits, because writing a well-researched editorial on the psychology of fanboyism is significantly harder to promote than a stupid clickbait article meant to confirm the biases and fulfill the wishes of people willing to click.

It's interesting how you bring up the relationship between publishers and the press- you're totally right that it's a business relationship! It's the worst-kept secret in the industry. I'm actually writing a book for indie developers right now on how to deal with the press, and something I talk about is how, when developers reciprocate coverage- just retweeting it, for instance- it makes a difference to the outlet and may result in further coverage. Kinda gross? I think so, and I'm a journo- but sadly, it's increasingly necessary due to the changing media landscape. I'm not sure if you've ever tried to make a living with ad revenue, let me tell you, it's near impossible. You have to be driving in massive traffic before you break even! Pulling people into a site is a full-time job in itself.

That's why I, in large part, have given up on some of the more traditional aspects of game journalism. If a publisher announce a TRIPLE XP WEEKEND or they post a new trailer or what have you, I don't go to the trouble of re-posting it. It's not worth the time or effort. Instead, I try to spend more of my time doing worthwhile stuff, like writing reviews and in-depth editorials- something that brings value to the table. Not that there's no value to knowing about those sweet XP bonuses, but guess what? Somebody else is already posting that stuff.

Anyway, what I'm saying is that while game journalism very definitely has its problems, withholding review copies isn't going to lead to better coverage, and it's not going to fix the problems- it's going to exacerbate them. Less scrupulous outlets will rush coverage out the door on day one, honest outlets will be late and lose the views snatched up by the unscrupulous outlets, and so if there are serious issues with the game- the sort of stuff that you'd notice after playing for a week instead of a day- it's not going to wind up in the less honest but more clicked-on reviews.
